title: After 15 Years, Mathematicians Invent the World's Fairest Dice
summary:
Imagine rolling a die to decide who goes first in a board game — but instead of a boring six-sided cube, you pick up a 60-sided sphere. And instead of just one, there are five, each engraved with numbers from 1 to 300. That's the invention mathematicians just unveiled after 15 years of work.

The quest began around 2010 at a gaming convention. Board game designer James Ernest asked his friend Eric Harshbarger, a mathematician at Auburn University, a deceptively simple question: Could you design a set of dice so that any number of players — two, three, five, whatever — could each grab one, roll, and have a perfectly equal shot at going first? No ties, no rerolls.

Harshbarger didn't have an answer that night, but the problem stuck. Over the next 15 years, he and a network of collaborators chipped away at what became known as the "go first dice" problem. The easy part was avoiding ties — just put different numbers on each die. The hard part was distributing those numbers so that fairness held for any subset of players. "The problem comes in how you distribute those different numbers across the dice so that the probability is equal not only for the whole set but for any subset," Harshbarger explained.

Early breakthroughs came quickly. Within weeks, they had a three-player solution using standard six-sided dice. Later, four 12-sided dice worked for four players. But five players required something much bigger — and the search space was astronomically huge. "We're talking literally more than the number of atoms in the universe — like 10 to the 128th power combinations," Harshbarger said. Even with all the computers and AI imaginable, brute force was impossible.

They needed mathematical shortcuts — symmetries and patterns to shrink the search space. Years passed. Then, in mid-2023, Canadian software engineer Paul Meyer emailed Harshbarger out of the blue. He'd been studying patterns in the four-player data and had written a program to exploit them. It worked.

The result: five 60-sided dice, collectively covering every number from 1 to 300, with no repeats. The dice don't just decide who goes first — they determine the entire turn order, with every possible sequence equally likely. That property, called permutation fairness, is what makes them truly remarkable.

To celebrate, Harshbarger built giant wooden replicas of the dice, now on permanent display at Auburn's new mathematics building. So next time you're stuck arguing over who goes first, remember: math has your back.
why_it_matters: This isn't just about board games; fair-random-order problems appear in sports draws, online matchmaking, and scheduling, so a way to guarantee fairness for every subgroup could inspire algorithms that affect how tournaments and competitions are organised. It also shows that a simple question can take a decade of creative teamwork to solve.

background_read: Rolling dice to choose who goes first is supposed to be simple, but a die is only fair if every face has the same chance of landing up.
The 'go-first dice' problem asked whether any number of players could grab one die from a set, roll once, and end up with a fair order and no ties.
James Ernest, a board game designer, posed the question to Eric Harshbarger, a mathematician at Auburn University (a public research university in Alabama).
The search turned out to belong to combinatorics, the branch of mathematics that studies arrangements, combinations, and counting.

Paul Meyer, a software engineer in Canada, eventually supplied the decisive shortcut after spotting patterns in earlier four-player dice data — an example of progress made by a curious outsider rather than a university research team.

perspectives.description: For players and game designers, the new dice solve an annoying real-life problem: a fair way to decide turn order without ties, rerolls, or outside rules. Making the dice physical also means the proof can sit on a table and be rolled.

Some critics will say the five 60-sided dice are too strange for ordinary board games. Large engraved spheres are hard to read in low light and would be expensive to mass-produce, so the mathematical victory may stay mostly symbolic.

Looked at mathematically, the achievement is about shrinking an impossible search space using patterns. Rather than finding one lucky arrangement, the authors found a class of arrangements that satisfies fairness for every subset of players.

The natural open question is what happens with six, seven, or more players. Future work may also apply the pattern-searching method to other scheduling and ranking problems where whole-system fairness is too complex for brute force.
